subject: marginal likelihood for coefficients of a linear regression

messages.author: 484c91357ac83f6b
messages.subject: marginal likelihood for coefficients of a linear regression
parts:
Suppose I want to get the ratio of marginal likelihood of:

H0: regression has only coefficient beta1
and
H1: regression has coefficients beta1 and beta2

What would be the correct approach using discrete parameter marginalization:

(Approach 1)
...
parameters {
real beta1;
real beta2;
}
transformed parameters {
real lp[2];
lp[1] <- normal_log(y, x1*beta1);
lp[2] <- normal_log(y, x1*beta1 + x2*beta2);
}
model {
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));
}
generated quantities {
int<lower=1,upper=2> H;
H <- categorical_rng(softmax(lp));
}
...

or


(Approach 2)
...
parameters {
real beta11;
real beta21;
real beta22;
}
transformed parameters {
real lp[2];
lp[1] <- normal_log(y, x1*beta11);
lp[2] <- normal_log(y, x1*beta21 + x2*beta22);
}
model {
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));
}
generated quantities {
int<lower=1,upper=2> H;
H <- categorical_rng(softmax(lp));
}
...

?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] marginal likelihood for coefficients of a linear regression
parts:
I'm not sure what you're trying to do, but then I don't know
much about model comparison. If you want the Bayesian posterior
on a likelihood ratio, you need to estimate the two likelihoods
separately. So you'll need to parameterize separately with beta1a,
beta1b, beta2b. Then each will fit separately as normal. A regression
coefficient isn't fixed when there are other predictors.

Then you could make a mixture model and estimate the mixing ratio,
which is what you seem to be doing. But you'll need the mixture proportion.
There's a log_mix function that'll help.

Or you could just compute the likelihood ratio and save it as a generated
quantity (or transformed parameter).

- Bob
